claims.text: On 2026-01-07, the patient presented with a severe headache rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sudden onset after exertion, throbbing, diffuse, and associated with mild nausea but no vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, or neck stiffness.
The patient has no past medical history, takes no medications, and reports no allergies.

Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent in daily activities, works as a primary school teacher, does not smoke, consumes approximately 6 units of alcohol per week, and engages in regular jogging.
Family history is negative for cerebrovascular accidents, aneurysms, or migraines, though the mother has type 2 diabetes and the father has hypertension.

Initial observations on 2026-01-07 recorded a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg, heart rate of 88 bpm, respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min, temperature of 36.7-36.8°C, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air.

Initial neurological examinations on 2026-01-07 were unremarkable, showing the patient alert and oriented with no focal deficits, normal cranial nerves, intact motor and sensory function, no neck stiffness, and unremarkable fundoscopy.
A CT head scan performed at 14:45 on 2026-01-07 showed no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage or mass lesion.
Blood tests collected at 15:15 on 2026-01-07 revealed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L), CRP of 8 mg/L, and normal renal and liver function tests.
On 2026-01-07, the diagnosis of Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS) was suspected based on clinical presentation and CT findings, and the patient was admitted to the Neurology ward.
On 2026-01-07, the treatment plan included starting oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours and arranging MRI/MRA of the brain and cerebral vasculature.
On 2026-01-07, the patient reported persistent headache rated 7/10, with blood pressure at 150/92 mmHg, and blood tests showed mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) and marginally elevated CRP (12 mg/L).
On 2026-01-07, the plan was to continue nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours and add oral potassium chloride 1 g twice daily to correct hypokalemia.
On 2026-01-07 at 20:00, the patient's GP was contacted to provide an update on admission and the preliminary diagnosis of RCVS.
On 2026-01-08, MRI/MRA confirmed the diagnosis of RCVS, headache severity reduced to 5/10, blood pressure was 135/85 mmHg, CRP was 12 mg/L, and mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) persisted.
On 2026-01-08, the medication regimen was adjusted to nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours, and potassium chloride 1 g twice daily was continued.
On 2026-01-08, a repeat MRA was planned for 48 hours later to assess resolution of vasoconstriction.
On 2026-01-08, the patient received education on RCVS, including avoidance of triggers such as intense physical exertion, stress, triptans, and ergotamines.
On 2026-01-09, headache severity further reduced to 3/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and blood tests from the previous day showed mild hyponatremia (sodium 132 mmol/L).
On 2026-01-09, the plan included increasing oral sodium intake through dietary measures, restricting excessive fluid intake, and repeating MRA in 24 hours.
On 2026-01-09, the rehab team assessed the patient, noting mild residual neck stiffness but no significant functional impairments, and arranged for outpatient physiotherapy post-discharge.
On 2026-01-10, headache intensity was 2/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L) was noted on previous tests.
On 2026-01-10, the plan was to maintain nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours, continue dietary measures for hyponatremia, and perform a repeat MRA on 2026-01-11.
On 2026-01-10, the patient was provided with a discharge planning booklet covering RCVS management, lifestyle modifications, and warning signs.
On 2026-01-11, headache symptoms were rated 2/10, blood pressure was 125/78 mmHg, and the patient was adhering to the management plan.
On 2026-01-11, the plan was to continue nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours and perform a repeat MRA to confirm resolution of vasoconstriction.
On 2026-01-11 at 10:30, a repeat MRA showed significant improvement in cerebral vasoconstriction, confirming the diagnosis of RCVS.
On 2026-01-11, discharge planning was initiated for 2026-01-12, with outpatient neurology follow-up arranged for 4 weeks post-discharge.
On 2026-01-12, the patient reported no further headaches, blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, and mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L) was noted.
On 2026-01-12, the patient was discharged with a prescription for nimodipine 30 mg orally four times daily to be tapered over 2 weeks, and a referral for neurology outpatient follow-up in 4 weeks.
On 2026-01-12 at 12:00, the patient's GP was contacted to discuss discharge, and a discharge medication of amlodipine 5 mg once daily was discussed.
Medication records conflict regarding the discharge regimen: note-17 documents nimodipine 30 mg four times daily to be tapered over 2 weeks, while note-18 documents amlodipine 5 mg once daily.
